title: AI and Spiritual Evolution
author: Rupert Wegerif
summary: Rupert Wegerif answers the worry that AI will make students less intelligent by arguing that the worry rests on a print-shaped idea of intelligence as the manipulation of texts, concepts and procedures. Drawing on his classroom research with Neil Mercer on the Thinking Together programme, he shows a girl named Trisha moving from stubborn assertion to a moment of insight when she realises you must take the circle out of a pattern. He uses that scene to separate the living process of understanding from the reified products it leaves behind, and to describe a dialogue with an implicit witness that holds our thinking answerable to reality. Spirit is defined as lived openness to a larger reality, not an opposite of intellect, and he cites Aquinas on ratio and intellectus to support the point. Because AI is good at handling the products of past understanding, he suggests schools could shift time toward inquiry, discussion, observation and making. He closes by insisting that AI will not deliver spiritual growth by itself and that the outcome depends on educational choices.
points: The fear that AI weakens thinking assumes intelligence means processing texts, an assumption inherited from print literacy that Wegerif asks readers to question.
The Trisha and George episode illustrates that insight comes before the rule that expresses it, so education that targets only the rules confuses the product with the process.
Dialogue works through an implicit witness, a perspective beyond either speaker that makes each person's thinking answerable to the thing being understood.
Because AI handles the stored products of understanding well, schools could redirect time from memorising and reproducing toward inquiry, discussion and wondering about the world.
Knowledge still matters, so AI's role is to supply just enough knowledge at the right moment to fuel discovery, and whether it helps depends on educational choices.
quotes: There is another side to thinking and learning that is harder to capture and measure. This is the experience of insight: the moment when something that was previously obscure suddenly becomes clear.
Because so much of education has been built around print, we have come to mistake the skills of print literacy for intelligence itself.
There is an important distinction here between the living process of understanding and the products it leaves behind.

Much of education focuses on these products: concepts, procedures, explanations and arguments. We turn the living process of discovery into fixed forms of knowledge that can be transmitted and assessed.
Spirit is our lived openness to a larger reality, a relationship with possibilities of meaning that draw us beyond ourselves.

AI is particularly good at handling the products of past understanding: texts, concepts, arguments and explanations. If it can take on more of this, schools could give much more time to the parts of education that bring understanding to life, such as inquiry, discussion, observation, making things and wondering about the world.
AI will not bring about spiritual evolution by itself. That depends on the educational choices we make.
